name: Sam Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a shopfitter, which means I build the insides of shops, cafés and restaurants, the counters, shelving, wall panels, changing rooms. I work for Keystone Interiors, and most of our jobs are in the big shopping centre in the city, forty minutes from home. A lot of it is nights, because the shops want to stay open in the day, so I start at ten and finish at six in the morning. I like walking past a café I built and seeing people sat at my counter. The nights wear me down, and you never feel properly rested on your days off.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Nights at the shopping centre. What's home like around that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Nadia's a care assistant, she does early shifts, so some weeks we pass each other in the hallway like ships. Our girls are grown, Yasmin's an accountant and Leila manages a phone shop, and we've got a little grandson, Adam, who's four. Money's tight, Nadia's hours got cut last year and we've got maybe three weeks of savings. Keystone is about the only shopfitter around that still takes on men my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, that's that then. At work we'd have a laugh about all the robots that never came. I'm not much for posting, but I might send a joke to the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's no different. The shops still need fitting, Keystone still gets the work, I keep doing nights. The worry was always more about shops closing, and that's online shopping, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Keystone and maybe try to get onto more day jobs as I get older. I already use one of those chat programs now and then, Yasmin set it up, to work out how many sheets of board a job needs, so I'd keep that. And I'd keep trying to build a bit of savings, even a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the life I know, tiring but steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a chat program to work out board quantities. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yasmin saw me doing sums on the back of a delivery note at her kitchen table and laughed. She typed my measurements into her phone and it gave the answer in five seconds. I checked it by hand, it was right, so now I use it when I remember. I still check it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said shops closing worries you. Have you seen that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Plenty. In the shopping centre there are three empty units on the top floor that I fitted out myself. One was a shoe shop, one a bookshop, one a card shop. When I walk past them on nights, it's like visiting graves.

S0.say: Well, that's that then, and we'd have a laugh at work about the robots that never came. I might send a joke to the family group.
S0.think: It's no different for me, the shops still need fitting. The worry was always shops closing because of online shopping, not AI.
S0.do: Carries on at Keystone and tries for more day work as he gets older. Keeps using the chat program his daughter set up for board quantities and tries to save about a hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm, because it's the life he knows, tiring but steady.
S0.quote: When I walk past them on nights, it's like visiting graves.
S0.fieldNote: Sam sees his job as tied to the health of shops, not to AI itself. He already uses a chatbot a little but always double-checks it, which fits his steady nature. In this picture he's calm, though the empty units he built clearly stay with him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say you've got to move with it, but carefully. At work I'd tell the lads to see what's actually useful before panicking. To friends I'd say the government should keep an eye on it, but not stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think shopfitting is safer than a lot of jobs, because every shop is different and the units are never square. What I'd worry about is fewer shops overall, and Yasmin, because accounting is exactly the kind of thing these programs do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the others at Keystone started using the new drawing apps, I'd learn them too, I'm not proud. I'd keep putting the hundred a month away, maybe stretch to one fifty if Nadia's hours come back. I'd ask Keystone whether there's a maintenance contract in the shopping centre I could move onto, because that's steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for Yasmin than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yasmin?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her she's clever and she'll find her way, which is true. But I'd also say, think about what parts of your job a machine can't do, like sitting with a worried shop owner and explaining their taxes. She'd roll her eyes and say Dad, I know. She always knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a maintenance contract. What would that job be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shopping centre has a small team that fixes doors, ceiling tiles, broken benches, anything that goes wrong. It's day work, less money, but steady, and they're always short. Gary runs it, I've known him fifteen years. It's my plan B, I suppose.

S1.say: You've got to move with it, but carefully. The government should keep an eye on it, but not stop it.
S1.think: Shopfitting is safer than a lot of jobs because every unit is different and never square. I'd worry more about fewer shops overall and about my daughter, since accounting is exactly what these programs do.
S1.do: Learns the new drawing apps once his colleagues have started using them and keeps saving a hundred a month, more if his wife's hours return. Asks Keystone about moving onto the shopping centre's maintenance team as a steady plan B.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for his daughter than for himself.
S1.quote: She'd roll her eyes and say Dad, I know. She always knows.
S1.fieldNote: He takes a classic steady stance, learning once others have. His main worry is not his own job but his daughter's office work, which he sees as more exposed. He has a quiet plan B lined up with a man he's known for fifteen years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and somebody should have slowed it down. At work I'd say we'll see who's still standing. I'd probably keep it off social media, people just argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's frightening. I'd be 60, three weeks of savings, and if robots can build a counter and nobody needs shops anyway, Keystone's gone. Yasmin's job would go even faster, so I couldn't lean on her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go straight to Gary about the maintenance team while there's still a chance. Nadia and I would cut back hard, the car insurance down to the basic, no holidays, nothing extra. I'd do handyman jobs at weekends for people on our street, shelves, doors, flat-pack, cash in hand, whatever brings a bit in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that, with only two years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake after night shifts, which is the worst kind of awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you couldn't lean on Yasmin. Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's brother has a bit of money, he runs a restaurant. I fitted his place for nothing years ago. I'd hate to ask, but I would, if it meant keeping the flat. And the mosque has a fund for families in trouble, we've given to it, we might need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those two years look like before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody knows what to believe at first, I think. The shops would carry on until they don't. I'd take every night shift Keystone offers to build up some money, and I'd be checking the news on my breaks like everyone else.

S2.say: This is too fast and somebody should have slowed it down. At work I'd say we'll see who's still standing, and I'd keep it off social media.
S2.think: At 60 with three weeks of savings, if robots build counters and nobody needs shops, Keystone is gone. My daughter's job would go even faster, so I couldn't lean on her.
S2.do: Goes straight to the shopping centre's maintenance team about a job and takes every night shift in the two years before. Cuts car insurance and holidays, and does weekend handyman jobs for neighbours, while turning to his brother-in-law and the mosque fund if needed.
S2.feel: Alarmed, lying awake after night shifts.
S2.quote: I'd be lying awake after night shifts, which is the worst kind of awake.
S2.fieldNote: His plan B and his family safety net are both weaker in this picture, because the shops and his daughter's job would go too. He'd turn to community and extended family rather than the state. His pragmatism holds, but the fear is clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years, that's time to get ready if people are sensible. At work I'd tell the younger ones to pick up skills now. I'd still keep it off social media.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to 63. If I can get onto Gary's maintenance team in the next year or two and learn whatever they use there, I might ride it out until the pension. It's tight, but it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gary for a place in the first year, even part-time at first. I'd learn the building management system they use, the computer that runs the lights and doors, once someone showed me. And I'd put the weekend handyman money straight into savings, not spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does that feel compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but there's a path, and I like having a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Learning a building management system at 59. How do you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I learned the chat program, didn't I? If Gary sat with me for a week, I'd get it. I'm not the fastest, but I'm careful, and in maintenance careful matters more than fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for Yasmin with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd have time to move into something else, maybe advising small businesses face to face. I'd tell her to start now, not wait. With five years I think she'd be fine, she's sharper than me.

S3.say: Five years is time to get ready if people are sensible. I'd tell the younger ones to pick up skills now.
S3.think: By 63, if I'm on the maintenance team and know their systems, I might ride it out until the pension. It's tight, but possible.
S3.do: Asks for a maintenance team place in the first year, even part-time. Learns the building management system once someone shows him, and puts all weekend handyman money into savings.
S3.feel: Anxious, but glad to have a path.
S3.quote: I'm not the fastest, but I'm careful, and in maintenance careful matters more than fast.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns his plan B into a real plan. He's honest about being nervous to learn the centre's systems but points to the chatbot as proof he can. His worry for his daughter eases with more time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people will sort it out. I'd say it at work and at home. I'd probably not say much else, there's no point getting worked up a decade early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'm 68, so I'd likely be done. My worry would be whether the pension holds up and whether the girls are all right. For my own job, it's mostly a relief.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade's warning, what would you actually do, now and in the first year after it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Keystone and drift onto day work or the maintenance team in my early 60s. I'd keep saving what I can, a hundred, a hundred fifty. Mostly I'd wait and see, because ten years is long enough that half of what people predict won't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mainly for the girls. For myself, fairly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half of what people predict won't happen. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've heard it before. Twenty years ago they said nobody would shop in person by now, and I've fitted out more shops since than before. Things change, but slower and stranger than the experts say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Adam, your grandson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be fourteen in 2036. That's the one I really wonder about, what work there'll be for him. I'd tell him what my dad told me, learn to do something with your hands and your head, and be someone people trust.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty and people will sort it out. There's no point getting worked up a decade early.
S4.think: At 68 I'd likely be done, so for my own job it's mostly a relief. My worry is whether the pension holds and whether my daughters are all right.
S4.do: Keeps working at Keystone and moves onto day work or maintenance in his early sixties. Saves a hundred or a hundred and fifty a month and mostly waits to see, expecting many predictions to be wrong.
S4.feel: Uneasy for his daughters and grandson, fairly settled for himself.
S4.quote: Things change, but slower and stranger than the experts say.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years he relaxes, partly because he'd be past pension age and partly because he distrusts big predictions from experience. His worry moves to his grandson's future. He sees no reason to act dramatically so far ahead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. My plan B and my daughters would all get hit at once. What would help is if the government made employers give older workers a real chance at the new jobs, like the maintenance roles, before hiring young ones, and some help with income in between. Not charity, just a fair go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about nights. Half the trades people I know work nights now, and nobody thinks about what that does to a family. If robots end up doing the night shifts, honestly, that bit I wouldn't miss.

headlineQuote: If robots end up doing the night shifts, honestly, that bit I wouldn't miss.
portrait: Sam Rahman is a 58-year-old shopfitter who builds the insides of shops and cafés on night shifts in a city shopping centre, with about three weeks of savings since his wife's care hours were cut. He's steady and careful, uses a chatbot his daughter set up but always checks it, and keeps a quiet plan B on the centre's maintenance team. He's calm in the Plateau and uneasy in Steady Disruption, worried more for his accountant daughter than himself. AGI by 2028 alarms him because his plan B, the shops and his family safety net would all go at once, while five and ten years leave him room to switch and wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because his plan B and his daughters would all be hit at once.
whatWouldHelp: A fair chance for older workers at the new roles before younger hires, and some income help in between.
